title_original: Zombucha! review – new Australian zombie film never quite finds its bite
excerpt_original: An accident in kombucha brewing leads to a zombie outbreak in a movie which is a little too low-key to live up to its delicious potential Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email Zombucha! is a relatively rare example of a genre film that’s not really a genre film. There are…

blocks.text: Z ombucha! is a relatively rare example of a genre film that’s not really a genre film. There are zombies in it, caused by an accident in kombucha brewing, but they arrive relatively late in the game – and anybody expecting flesh-chewing carnage will probably leave disappointed. Nor is the film a vehicle for social commentary, despite the premise having some delicious potential for wellness industry satire.

What we do get is an enjoyably staged and well-paced production that’s never boring, despite the long wait for the main action. There’s also something kind of endearing about a zombie film so low-key it almost forgets to be a zombie film. Emma Leonard’s writing, Claudia Dzienny’s direction and the performances are all appealing, albeit lacking some flair. I was consistently entertained but will probably never return for a rewatch.

Set and shot on Sydney’s northern beaches, the film is an Australian production with a predominantly New Zealand cast, making it feel oddly unmoored and culturally adrift. It begins outdoors at night, cinematic mist hanging in the air while some (supposedly) undead folk stagger around. “This one’s mine,” says a woman, who delivers an almighty kick to a flesh-chewer. This scene feels a bit dodgy for good reason: we’re watching the set of a zombie movie rather than a zombie movie (this conceit perhaps invites comparison with the 2017 Japanese movie One Cut the Dead , a masterpiece of daffy meta inventiveness). It’s also the workplace of Maddie (Leonard), a makeup artist who is fired after accidentally poisoning one of the principal cast.

Meanwhile, her husband, Leo (Ryan O’Kane), the creative director at an advertising agency, is getting great feedback from clients – his ad for an energy drink considered “poetic” and “paradigm-shifting”. But he’s tired of working crazy long hours for the “toxic capitalist machine”, despite some generous perks from his boss Hopper (Jackie van Beek), such as a bag of white powder to help him power through. So Leo quits his job, which Maddie isn’t thrilled about, given she lost hers on the same day and the pair are “mortgaged up to the freakin’ eyeballs”.

Ambling through a farmers’ market and encountering a flaky kombucha vendor (Stephen Madsen), they get an idea to start their own line, stealing the main ingredients: the vendor’s scoby and a sprig of greenery from their nextdoor neighbour (Brigid Zengeni). The combination of these ingredients leads to the drink somehow causing an outbreak of you-know-what (don’t overthink it). But “outbreak” might be overstating it, given the body count remains rather low: this production is, even in its whackier moments, a rather modest affair. In terms of its incongruous combination of everyday, domestic vibes and moaning flesh-chewers, the obvious point of comparison is Edgar Wright’s Shaun of the Dead , though that film is much more upbeat and action-packed (and has better special effects; the creature design here is fine, but lacks panache).

blocks.caption: ‘Zombucha! feels less quirky than absent-minded: an amiable affair that never quite finds its bite.’ Photograph: Boobytrap Entertainment

blocks.text: Emma Leonard and Ryan O’Kane are likeable leads, able to lighten potentially heavy moments with splashes of levity. Like Dzienny’s direction, they strike a good balance between self-awareness and sincerity, even if their characters are a little thinly layered. The performance that pops the most comes from the always entertaining Jackie van Beek, though as the film’s MVP, her role is disappointingly small.

There are some elements that might’ve given Zombucha! a little more impact had the film developed them more, such as the central couple’s fear of having a child. The film ends up feeling less quirky than absent-minded: an amiable affair that never quite finds its bite.
